stem: A dependent client requires repositioning in bed. Which nursing action best reflects current safe-patient-handling guidance?

options.A: Assess the client's current mobility and the repositioning task, follow the handling plan, and use the indicated assistive device with trained staff rather than relying on unsupported manual force.
options.B: Begin with a manual two-person repositioning attempt and bring in patient-handling equipment if the client cannot tolerate the turn or the staff members cannot complete it comfortably.
options.C: Use the unit's usual number of helpers and the same repositioning method used previously, without reassessing mobility unless the client reports new pain or weakness during the move.
options.D: Use a drawsheet and careful body mechanics as the primary approach when mechanical or other assistive handling equipment is available, adding the equipment after a difficult manual attempt.

rationale: Current NIOSH guidance identifies manual lifting, moving, and repositioning of patients as the greatest work-related musculoskeletal-disorder risk factor for healthcare workers and recommends safe-patient-handling and mobility technology, established procedures, and training. OSHA identifies bed repositioning as a high-risk patient-handling task and states that safe patient handling should include care planning, hazard and task assessment, appropriate patient-handling devices, and staff training. OSHA also emphasizes that each patient's mobility characteristics and abilities should be systematically assessed and that equipment should be selected for the specific lifting, transfer, and movement need. Therefore A is correct. B makes an unsupported manual attempt the default before using equipment. C substitutes habit for reassessment of the client's current mobility and the task. D relies on manual handling first even when appropriate assistive technology is available, contrary to the equipment-based risk-control approach described by NIOSH and OSHA.
educational_objective: For dependent-client repositioning, assess the client's current mobility and the handling task, follow the care plan and safe-handling procedure, and use appropriate assistive technology with trained staff rather than defaulting to unsupported manual repositioning.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH); Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
source_document_title: About Safe Patient Handling and Mobility; Healthcare — Safe Patient Handling; Worker Safety in Hospitals — Facility and Patient Needs Assessment
source_version_date: NIOSH page dated May 9, 2024 and current at access 2026-08-25; current OSHA Safe Patient Handling resources accessed 2026-08-25
source_locator: NIOSH About Safe Patient Handling and Mobility > Overview: patient handling includes manual lifting, moving, and repositioning; patient handling is the single greatest WMSD risk factor for healthcare workers. > Prevention steps and strategies: provide and use assistive lifting devices, follow established procedures, and participate in training. OSHA Healthcare — Safe Patient Handling: repositioning side-to-side in bed and lifting/repositioning a patient in bed are high-risk tasks; effective programs include hazard assessment, care planning, appropriate patient-handling devices, and staff training. OSHA Worker Safety in Hospitals — Facility and Patient Needs Assessment > Patient Needs Assessments and Algorithms: each patient's characteristics and mobility abilities should be systematically assessed and the plan of care adapted to mobility needs with appropriate technology and methods.
source_claim_supported: Safe repositioning requires assessment of the patient's mobility and the handling task, use of appropriate patient-handling technology and established procedures, and trained staff rather than routine unsupported manual handling.

supporting_sources.locator: Safe Patient Handling overview: repeated manual patient handling, including repositioning patients, is a major source of musculoskeletal injury; high-risk tasks include side-to-side bed repositioning and lifting/repositioning in bed. Effective programs include hazard/task assessment, care planning, patient-handling devices, staff training, and program evaluation.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Bed repositioning is a high-risk handling task and should be managed through task assessment, care planning, appropriate equipment, and training rather than default manual handling.

supporting_sources.document_title: Worker Safety in Hospitals — Facility and Patient Needs Assessment
supporting_sources.locator: Patient Needs Assessments and Algorithms: every patient has unique characteristics and abilities that should be assessed regularly; systematic mobility assessment protects patients and caregivers, and the plan of care should specify appropriate technology and methods.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: The handling method should be individualized to the patient's current mobility and care-plan needs rather than selected by habit or a fixed staffing rule.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort, printed p. 35: assess client performance of activities of daily living and assist when needed; assist client to compensate for a physical or sensory impairment using assistive devices or positioning; implement measures to promote circulation including positioning and mobilization. Related Assistive Devices content includes assessing and managing client use of assistive devices and evaluating correct use.
blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — safe repositioning, positioning, mobilization, and use of assistive handling technology
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four actions to remove the distractor-only absolute wording and keyed-answer length cue. The revised distractors test realistic unsafe practices: manual-first handling, habit-based staffing/method selection without reassessment, and reliance on body mechanics or a drawsheet before available assistive technology.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Safe patient handling — dependent-client bed repositioning
audit_findings.stem: PASS — specifies dependency and a concrete high-risk handling task without prescribing an unsupported fixed number of helpers or a universal device.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly reflects current NIOSH/OSHA guidance to assess mobility and task requirements, follow the handling plan, use indicated technology, and rely on trained staff; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — two-person assistance can be appropriate in some circumstances, but making a manual attempt the default before indicated equipment ignores the technology-first risk-control approach and patient-specific plan.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — consistency may be useful, but safe handling requires current mobility/task assessment rather than selecting helper count and technique by unit habit until symptoms occur.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — drawsheet use and body mechanics may be components of some handling plans, but using manual handling as the default before available indicated assistive technology does not reflect current SPHM guidance.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option that integrates patient-specific assessment, task assessment, the established handling plan, appropriate technology, and trained assistance without imposing a universal staffing count or manual-first trial.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B and D default to manual handling before equipment; C omits current reassessment and task-based selection.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all options are comparable in length and procedural detail; the keyed answer is not uniquely long and no distractor-only absolute term remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Basic Care and Comfort directly includes ADL assistance, positioning, mobilization, and assistive-device use.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether two-person manual repositioning or careful body mechanics could be accepted as the primary strategy. NIOSH and OSHA identify manual repositioning as a major ergonomic risk and emphasize systematic patient/task assessment, care planning, equipment, and training; A remains uniquely best while avoiding an unsupported universal device or staffing number.
